**(C)** Sporophyte

Pteridophytes show heteromorphic alternation of generations in which the sporophyte is diploid, dominant, autotrophic and independent, with true roots, stem and leaves. Their gametophyte is small, haploid and short lived. A capsule is the sporophyte of a bryophyte, and the embryo is only the first stage of the sporophyte, not a phase of the life cycle.

**(A)** *Sequoia sempervirens*

The chapter states that *Sequoia sempervirens*, the coast redwood of California, is the tallest living plant in the world, about 366 feet high. *Taxodium mucronatum* is famous for its girth (about 125 feet), not its height, *Zamia pygmaea* is the smallest gymnosperm at about 25 cm, and *Ginkgo biloba* is known as a living fossil.

**(B)** Sporophyte is partially dependent upon gametophyte

In bryophytes the haploid gametophyte is the dominant, photosynthetic, independent plant body, while the sporophyte (foot, seta and capsule) is short lived and depends totally or partially on the gametophyte for nutrition and anchorage. So the two generations are not independent, the gametophyte does not depend on the sporophyte, and the gametophyte is the conspicuous plant, not an inconspicuous one.

**(D)** Double fertilization

Double fertilization, in which one male gamete fuses with the egg and the other with the secondary nucleus to form the endosperm, takes place only in angiosperms, so it is the feature that marks the group. Seed formation is shared with gymnosperms, collateral vascular bundles are found in the stems of gymnosperms as well, and radial vascular bundles are a feature of roots in general, not of angiosperms alone.

[Note: the chapter only names double fertilization in a recall question; standard biology gives that it is found in angiosperms alone.]

**(D)** Enclosed seed

The name Angiospermae means enclosed seed: their seeds develop inside the ovary, which becomes the fruit, while gymnosperms bear naked seeds on megasporophylls. Both groups are autotrophic, and both carry pollen to the egg through a pollen tube (siphonogamy). The chapter says gymnosperm xylem has predominantly tracheids, so vessels are a usual but not an absolute difference.

[Note: the chapter does not discuss vessels in detail; standard biology gives that a few gymnosperms such as *Gnetum* do have vessels, so the enclosed seed is the difference that always holds.]
